540.title: Chitrakoot
540.hook: you can still walk barefoot around the hill where the exiles lived
540.howItsDone: Pilgrims at Chitrakoot bathe at Ram Ghat on the Mandakini and walk the parikrama, the circuit around Kamadgiri hill, often barefoot, especially on new-moon days.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot, the bright mountain, a house of leaves, and Valmiki inside his own story. Did you notice your own front door? A new week begins, and today we visit Chitrakoot as it is now. Day five hundred forty.
screen: `A PARNASHALA, A HOUSE OF LEAVES.`

segments.voice: Most stories happen in places you can't go. Nobody can buy a ticket to Middle-earth. But on the border of two Indian states, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, there's a small town called Chitrakoot, with a green hill, a river and a lot of temples. Every day, pilgrims arrive there, take off their shoes, and start walking. They're walking around the hill where, they believe, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana once lived in a hut of leaves.
screen: `PLACES YOU CAN'T GO.` → `A TOWN CALLED CHITRAKOOT.` → `PILGRIMS TAKE OFF THEIR SHOES.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Chitrakuta is made of two Sanskrit words: chitra, bright, wonderful, many-colored, and kuta, a peak. The bright peak. In Hindi it's usually said Chitrakoot. Valmiki names a river there too, the Mandakini, and today the Mandakini still runs through the town. Its main bathing place is called Ram Ghat, and in the evenings people float lamps on the water. The hill at the center of the pilgrimage is called Kamadgiri, often explained as the hill that grants wishes. Pilgrims walk all the way around it, often barefoot, stopping at shrines along the path. Walking around something holy, keeping it on your right, is called parikrama, and it's a way Hindus honor temples, rivers and hills alike. There's another layer. Chitrakoot is also linked with the poet Tulsidas, who retold the Ramayana in Hindi. A well-known tradition says that Tulsidas, sitting at Ram Ghat, was granted a vision of Rama there. So the town carries two Ramayanas at once: Valmiki's Sanskrit and Tulsidas's Hindi. Here's why that matters for our reading. The Ramayana isn't only a book. For pilgrims, its places are real places, and walking them is a way of reading the story with your feet. Scholars debate which modern sites match which verses, and the text doesn't settle every question. But the pilgrims aren't waiting for scholars. Every morning they take off their shoes, and they walk.
screen: `CHITRA AND KUTA: THE BRIGHT PEAK.` · `THE MANDAKINI AND RAM GHAT.` · `KAMADGIRI AND THE PARIKRAMA.` · `TULSIDAS'S VISION AT RAM GHAT.` · then, large: `READING THE STORY WITH YOUR FEET.`

segments.voice: Sit, and if you can, slip your shoes off, the way the pilgrims do at the foot of the hill. Feel the floor under your bare feet: how cool or warm it is, how hard, the places where it presses back. Let your breath slow. Keep your attention low, in the soles. Nothing to reach, nowhere to get to. Just this ground, and the breath moving over it. The bell holds the time.
Chitrakoot, today. A pilgrim town on the Mandakini, where people walk barefoot around Kamadgiri hill and read the Ramayana with their feet.

541.title: Chitrakoot
541.hook: Rama walks Sita around the mountain and tells her he doesn't miss the kingdom at all
541.tomorrow: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
541.howItsDone: In the text, the Mandakini at Chitrakuta is where Rama and Sita bathe; pilgrims to Chitrakoot bathe in the same river today.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot as it is today, a pilgrim town where people walk barefoot around the hill. Did you feel the ground under your feet? Today, the last look at the exiles' happy days on the mountain. Day five hundred forty-one.
screen: `READING THE STORY WITH YOUR FEET.`

segments.voice: Every hard story has a pause somewhere, a stretch where the characters get to simply live. On Chitrakuta, the exiles get theirs. The hut is built. The days fall into a rhythm: bathing in the river, gathering fruit, sitting by the fire at night. And one day Rama takes Sita by the hand and walks her around the mountain, pointing things out, the way you'd show someone the neighborhood you've just moved into and already love.
screen: `EVERY HARD STORY HAS A PAUSE.` → `A RHYTHM TO THE DAYS.` → `SHOWING HER THE NEIGHBORHOOD.`

segments.voice: Look at the peaks, Rama tells Sita: some silver, some red, some yellow like gold, some the color of crystal. Look at the waterfalls, the flowering trees, the birds. Then he says something tender and surprising. Seeing this mountain with you, I don't grieve for the kingdom, and I don't miss my friends. Living here, he says, brings him two good things: he keeps his father's word, and he gives his brother Bharata joy. He takes her down to the Mandakini river. Its water is clear. Sages are bathing in it, raising their arms to the sun. Deer come down to drink. Bathe here with me, Rama says. And he says, in effect: think of this mountain as Ayodhya, think of the deer as the people of the city, and think of the Mandakini as our own river Sarayu. You may hear an echo from a few days back. Sumitra told Lakshmana: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Now Rama tells Sita the same thing, and on the mountain, it's true. A small honest note about the text. Valmiki actually tells this scene a little later, while trouble is already on its way to the mountain, and the contrast is part of his art. We've placed it here, at the end of the exiles' first days, because it's the clearest picture of what those days were like. Now we go back to where Valmiki's story actually runs next. Far away in Ayodhya, the charioteer Sumantra is driving home, alone, with an empty chariot. And an old king is waiting.
screen: `SILVER, RED AND GOLDEN PEAKS.` · `I DON'T GRIEVE FOR THE KINGDOM.` · `THE MANDAKINI IS OUR SARAYU.` · `THE CAMERA TURNS TO AYODHYA.` · then, large: `AN EMPTY CHARIOT GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Pick one small place in your life where things are good right now, a corner, a routine, a person you're with. Settle into it in your mind, the way the exiles settled on the mountain. On each breath in, notice one good detail about it. On each breath out, let it be enough, just as it is, for now. The bell holds the time.

542.title: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
542.hook: an empty chariot comes home, and an old king finally tells a secret he has carried his whole life
542.carry: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
542.tomorrow: Dasharatha's death and the curse, part two
542.howItsDone: Ramayana reciters often tell Dasharatha's confession as its own episode, and later tellings know the young man as Shravan Kumar, in a children's story about care for parents.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot. Rama walked Sita around the mountain, showing her the river and the trees, and said he didn't miss the kingdom at all. Did you notice something you love about where you are? Today we go back to Ayodhya, where a chariot is coming home empty. Day five hundred forty-two.
screen: `A HUT ON THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Sumantra, the charioteer, drives back into Ayodhya alone. The horses are hanging their heads. The streets fill with people looking past him into the empty chariot, and then the wailing starts. He goes to the king and gives him Rama's messages, one by one. Dasharatha listens, and sinks into a grief deeper than before. That night, lying beside Kausalya, unable to sleep, he starts to talk. Not about Rama. About himself, long ago, when he was young, and very good with a bow.
screen: `AN EMPTY CHARIOT COMES HOME.` → `THE KING CAN'T SLEEP.` → `A STORY FROM LONG AGO.`

segments.voice: Dasharatha begins with a saying. Whatever a person does, good or bad, they eat its fruit later. Then he tells Kausalya what he has never told her. Before they were married, when he was still a prince, he was famous for one skill: he could shoot at a sound without seeing the target. The Sanskrit word for an archer like that is shabdavedhi, one who pierces by sound. One rainy season, he went out at night along the Sarayu river, hoping to catch an elephant or a buffalo coming down to drink. It was dark. He heard a gurgling at the water's edge, a heavy, deep sound, and he was sure it was an elephant drinking. He fitted an arrow, aimed at the sound, and let go. And from the water came a human voice. A cry of pain, and a question. Who would shoot an arrow at someone like me? I live in the forest, I harm no one, I only came for water. The young prince ran to the bank. There, half in the river, lay a young ascetic with matted hair, an arrow in his chest, and beside him a water pot, the thing that had made the sound. Dasharatha tells Kausalya he was shaking, his mind gone dark. Notice what the story is doing. A skill the young man was proud of, a guess made in the dark, a single shot that can't be called back. The old king has carried this since he was young, and tonight, with his son gone, he finally says it out loud.
screen: `WHAT YOU DO, YOU EAT LATER.` · `SHABDAVEDHI: HE SHOOTS AT SOUND.` · `A SOUND HE TOOK FOR AN ELEPHANT.` · `A WATER POT, AND A YOUNG ASCETIC.` · then, large: `ONE SHOT THAT CAN'T BE CALLED BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and close your eyes, or let them rest low. For this sit, just listen. Notice each sound around you, and notice how fast your mind names it: a car, a fan, a voice in the next room. Then let the label go and hear the sound itself, before the guess. 543.title: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
543.hook: a prince carries a water pot to a hut where two blind parents are waiting for their son
543.carry: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
543.tomorrow: Dasharatha's death and the curse, part three
543.howItsDone: This episode is often told on its own as a story about duty to parents, and about a prince who told a blind couple the truth instead of slipping away.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's death and the curse, part one. A young prince shot at a sound in the dark, and found a young ascetic with a water pot at the river. Did you catch yourself guessing before you looked? Day five hundred forty-three.
screen: `A SOUND IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: The young man in the river doesn't curse Dasharatha. That's the first surprise. He's dying, and what he talks about is his parents. They're old, he says, and both blind. They're sitting in a hut not far from here, thirsty, waiting for me to bring the water. Go to them. Tell them. And then he asks for one more thing: pull out the arrow. It's burning. The prince knows that if he pulls it, the boy will die. He does it anyway, because he was asked.
screen: `HE DOESN'T CURSE THE PRINCE.` → `MY PARENTS ARE BLIND AND THIRSTY.` → `PULL OUT THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: So Dasharatha fills the pot and walks the path the boy described. At the hut, the old father hears footsteps and speaks first. Why are you so late, son? Your mother was worried. Did we upset you? Say something. Picture the prince standing there with the water, hearing himself mistaken for the son he has just killed. And here is the moment the whole episode turns on. He could set the pot down and slip away. Nobody saw. Instead he tells them everything: who he is, the sound, the elephant he imagined, the arrow. In Valmiki's telling, the old father says something striking in reply. Because you told us yourself, he says, you are still alive. Had you hidden it, the consequences for you would have been far worse. The confession doesn't undo the death. But it changes what follows. The parents ask to be taken to their son. They sit with his body by the river, the mother and father touching his face, and they grieve aloud. The father then speaks the words that will shape the rest of Dasharatha's life. Just as I am losing my life in grief for my son, he says, you too will one day die grieving for a son. Then the old couple give up their lives on their son's funeral fire. Hold both halves of this. Telling the truth spared the young prince that night. It didn't spare him the curse. And tonight the old king is telling Kausalya that the curse is coming true. Rama is gone, and his father is dying of it. He knows exactly what's happening, because he was told long ago, by a father at a river.

segments.voice: Sit and let your breath slow down. Think of something small you once got wrong and never quite said out loud. Not the biggest thing. Something you can hold gently. Picture yourself telling it plainly to the person it touched, the way the prince told the old couple: what happened, nothing added, nothing hidden. You don't have to do anything about it today. Just notice how it feels to imagine saying it straight. The bell holds the time.

544.title: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
544.hook: a king dies at midnight, and a boy with no name in the oldest text becomes one of India's best-known sons
544.carry: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
544.howItsDone: Shravan Kumar is a common children's story across much of India, told to teach care for parents, and his name is still used as praise for a devoted son or daughter.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's death and the curse, part two. The prince told the blind parents the truth, and the father said: you too will die grieving for a son. Did you say something straight yesterday? Day five hundred forty-four.
screen: `YOU TOO WILL GRIEVE FOR A SON.`

segments.voice: In many Indian homes, children hear about the young man at the river long before anyone reads them the Ramayana. In those tellings he has a name, Shravan Kumar, and a picture to go with it: a son carrying his blind parents on a pilgrimage, one in each of two baskets hung from a pole across his shoulders. Grandparents tell it at bedtime as the story of a good son. So here's a small surprise. In Valmiki's Ramayana, the young man doesn't have a name, and there are no baskets. Both came later.
screen: `A NAME CHILDREN KNOW.` → `TWO BASKETS ON A POLE.` → `IN VALMIKI, NO NAME.`

segments.voice: The night ends. Dasharatha finishes the story, and he knows what it means. The curse is arriving. He tells Kausalya his eyes are failing, that he can't see her anymore. He says, in effect, if only Rama would come back and touch me now. He names the people who are lucky enough to see Rama's face when he returns. And somewhere past midnight, still speaking of his son, the old king dies. In the morning, the singers and attendants come to wake him as they always do, and find him gone. The palace breaks into grief. And because no son is there to perform the last rites, Rama in the forest and Bharata far away in his grandfather's kingdom, the ministers do something unusual. They lay the king's body in a vessel of oil, to keep it until Bharata can be brought home. Messengers ride for Kekaya with strict orders: say nothing of what has happened. Just bring him. Now the name. Valmiki calls the boy simply the young ascetic, the hermit's son. Later retellings, in regional languages and folk tradition, call him Shravana, or Shravan Kumar, and they add the picture of the baskets and the pilgrimage. The name fits him oddly well. Shravana is a Sanskrit word connected with hearing, and this is a boy killed by an archer who shot at a sound. So the story grew, over the centuries, around the one detail Valmiki left open, and the boy who had no name became a byword for loving your parents.

545.title: Bharata's journey
545.hook: a prince wakes from a bad dream, and riders arrive who won't tell him why they've come
545.howItsDone: Ramayana reciters tell Bharata's homecoming as its own episode: the dream, the silent city, and his first question, for Rama rather than the throne.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's death and the curse, part three. The king died past midnight, the body was kept in oil, and riders left for Kekaya with orders to say nothing. Did you reach out to someone older? Day five hundred forty-five.
screen: `RIDERS FOR KEKAYA.`

segments.voice: Far away, in his grandfather's city, Bharata wakes up badly shaken. His friends try to cheer him with music and jokes, and he can't smile. He tells them about the dream. His father, pale, hair loose, smeared with oil, riding a chariot pulled by donkeys, heading south. In the epics, the south is the direction of Yama, the lord of death. Bharata says: either I, or Rama, or Lakshmana, or the king is going to die. And that same day, the riders from Ayodhya arrive.
screen: `A DREAM IN KEKAYA.` → `A CHARIOT HEADING SOUTH.` → `THE RIDERS ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: The messengers do exactly as they were told. Your family's priest sends his greetings, they say. There's urgent business. Come at once. Bharata asks after everyone, one by one: his father, Rama, Lakshmana, the three queens. And the messengers give him careful, polite answers that are not quite answers. All is well, they say, with those you ask about. So he takes leave of his grandfather and sets out, and the journey home takes days. Valmiki gives us the road, the rivers crossed, the towns passed. And then Ayodhya appears, and something is wrong. No music. No crowds. The gardens look neglected, the streets are quiet, the people avoid his eyes. Bharata says to the charioteer: this isn't my city. He goes straight to his father's rooms, and his father isn't there. So he goes to his mother. Kaikeyi is glad to see him. She asks about the journey, about her family. And then she tells him, almost lightly: your father has gone the way all living things go. Bharata falls to the floor. When he can speak, he asks, where is Rama? I want to touch his feet. He's my father now. And Kaikeyi, believing she's giving him good news, tells him the rest: the two boons, the exile, the throne kept for him. She thinks she has made her son a king. She has no idea what she's about to hear back.

546.title: Bharata's journey
546.hook: the son a mother schemed for turns on her, and then has to convince another mother he never wanted any of it
546.howItsDone: Bharata is honored in Ramayana tradition as a model of loyalty and renunciation; his oaths before Kausalya run on for many verses of the Ayodhya Kanda.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharata's journey, part one. He came home to a silent city, and Kaikeyi told him, as if it were good news, that the throne was his. Did you read a room before you spoke? Today the week closes. Day five hundred forty-six.
screen: `SHE THINKS IT'S GOOD NEWS.`

segments.voice: Kaikeyi has been waiting for this conversation. Her son home, the crown ready. And what she gets is fury. Bharata doesn't thank her. He tells her she has destroyed the family, killed his father with grief, and sent away the brother he loves. He says the kingdom she won for him is something he will never accept. And then he walks out, to face the person he dreads most: Kausalya, Rama's mother.
screen: `NO THANKS, ONLY GRIEF.` → `I WILL NEVER ACCEPT IT.` → `NOW, KAUSALYA.`

segments.voice: Kausalya has every reason to suspect him. Here is the son who gains everything from her son's exile. She tells him so, bitterly: you wanted the kingdom, now you have it. Take me to Rama too. Bharata falls at her feet. And then he swears. Valmiki gives him a long chain of oaths, each one naming a wrong he'd rather be guilty of than this. May I carry the guilt of someone who betrays a trust, who strikes a sleeping person, who turns away a guest, if I ever wanted Rama gone. It goes on and on, a son emptying himself out. Kausalya believes him. She takes his head in her lap and they weep together. Then the duty that couldn't wait. Under Vasishtha's guidance, Bharata performs his father's funeral rites. The body is taken from the oil, the fire is lit, the queens and the city mourn, and the family offers water at the Sarayu. Afterward, at the palace, Shatrughna catches Manthara, the maid who started it all, and starts to drag her. Bharata stops him. Rama, he says, would never forgive us. Now the week. On Chitrakoot, a hut and a green hill, a sort of peace. In Ayodhya, a king's confession: a sound in the dark, a water pot, a father's curse. A death past midnight. A boy with no name who became Shravan Kumar. And this son, called home without being told, who refuses the prize his mother won for him.

segments.voice: Sit and let your shoulders drop. Think of a time someone suspected you of something you didn't do, or a time you suspected someone who turned out to be innocent. Don't argue it again. Just notice where it sits in your body: the jaw, the chest, the stomach. Breathe into that spot. On each out breath, let it loosen a little, the way Kausalya's suspicion loosened when she finally heard him. The bell holds the time.
